name: Vocal fry and glottal control

lead: Vocal fry is the lowest vocal register, a slow, creaky sound made with loose glottal closure. Some people learn to control it so their voice sounds lower.

The vocal folds are slack and compressed and vibrate slowly and irregularly, giving the low rattle. Research covers how fry is produced and how listeners react. A 2014 study reported that speakers using fry were rated less competent, less trustworthy and less attractive, though that study has been criticised for using imitators. No trials test fry as an appearance method.

paras: People use it at the ends of sentences or as a deliberate low register, usually practised with recordings to hear how it comes across. It is generally used in small amounts rather than as a constant speaking style.
Occasional use is generally considered normal, but excessive use may signal a voice disorder or tire the voice. Listener studies report mixed social perceptions.

social.title: Creaky Voice: Another Example of Young Women's Linguistic Ingenuity
Creaky Voice: Yet Another Example of Young Women's Linguistic Ingenuity

angle.text: Some people use controlled vocal fry to drop the sound of their voice into a lower, creakier register. It works by loosening glottal closure so the folds vibrate slowly. Perception studies of creaky voice exist and are mixed; none test it for vocal attractiveness.

lead: Vocal fry, also called creaky voice or glottal fry, is the lowest vocal register, produced with loose glottal closure that yields a slow, popping or rattling sound at very low frequency.[1] In looksmaxxing voice discussion, some people practise controlling it to reach lower notes and a lower-sounding voice, since voice is part of how a person is perceived alongside face and body.

Researchers describe fry as a normal production type on the pitch continuum and not by itself a pathology, though excessive use may signal a voice disorder.[1] Singers use it for very low notes outside modal voice, and vocal teachers use it to help students with low notes who carry excess laryngeal tension and breath pressure.[1] Some throat-singing styles, such as Tuvan kargyraa, use similar techniques.[1]

Studies of listener perception show mixed framing: a 2014 study by Anderson and colleagues reported that listeners rated young women using fry as less competent, less trustworthy and less attractive, though a critic has faulted its use of imitated fry.[1] No clinical studies were found testing fry as a method of appearance or voice enhancement.

paras: In fry, the arytenoid cartilages draw together, compressing the vocal folds so they become slack and form a large, irregularly vibrating mass; air bubbles through the loose closure.[1] When well controlled the register can extend far below modal voice.[1]

Fry has been linked to falling intonation in male Received Pronunciation speakers. Since the early 2000s researchers have reported it as more common among young American women, though the extent is disputed, and one 2010 study proposed that some young women adopt it to signal authority.[1] In some languages, such as Finnish and Jalapa Mazatec, creaky voice has structural roles.[1]

Fry is used for very low pitches unavailable in modal register, such as the croak at the start of phrases in some American country music, bass notes choirs borrow when true basses are scarce, and gospel bass singing.[1] Vocal pedagogues use it to help singers with low notes who have excess laryngeal tension.[1]

Anderson and colleagues (2014) reported negative ratings for speakers using fry, with stronger reactions among female evaluators; Rusty Barrett (2021) criticised the sample for using imitated fry.[1] A 2010 study found college-age listeners perceived creaky female voices as hesitant and informal but also educated and upwardly mobile, and a 2022 Finnish study found speakers without creaky voice rated as less fluent.[1] Some commentators argue such judgments reflect broader policing of women's voices.
Sources note that fry is not inherently a disorder, but excessive use may be, and some people seek speech pathologists because they feel it makes them sound unsure.[1]
No studies found testing fry or glottal control for appearance or for lowering everyday speaking pitch. Related research on listener perception and on fry in speech is summarised above.[1]
